teaser: A feared mercenary, dressed in pink silk in a Paris studio.
review_notes:
Gérôme's 1868 journey (Egypt, Sinai, Holy Land, Syria) lasting about twelve weeks; painted in Paris 1868-69 from a studio model dressed in textiles brought back: per the Met's catalog entry.
Married Marie Goupil (1863), daughter of dealer Adolphe Goupil; professor at the École des Beaux-Arts from 1864; attended the Suez Canal opening in 1869.
“Bashi-bazouk” translated as “headless” or “leaderless”; unpaid irregulars living off plunder.
Met acquired the painting in 2008.
Size about 81 x 66 cm.

lesson.text: By 1869, Jean-Léon Gérôme had little left to wish for. He was 45, a professor at the École des Beaux-Arts, the top art school in France. He had married the daughter of Adolphe Goupil, a dealer who sold prints of his pictures around the world. That November he was among the guests invited to Egypt for the opening of the Suez Canal.

The year before, he had spent about twelve weeks riding through Egypt, the Sinai desert and on to Jerusalem and Damascus. He came home with trunks of fabrics, clothes and weapons. Back in Paris, he dressed a model in the best of them and painted this.

A bashi-bazouk was an irregular soldier of the Ottoman Empire, the Turkish state that then ruled much of the Middle East. The name means roughly “headless”, as in leaderless. These men drew no pay and lived on what they looted. In European newspapers they stood for cruelty and disorder.
Now meet the man Gérôme actually painted. Start at the top.

spots.title: The headdress
spots.text: A red cap, then scarves wound in yellow, green and striped orange, hung with dozens of small tassels. It is as tall as his face again. Count the fabrics if you can.

spots.title: The profile
spots.text: Eyes half lowered, lips closed, head turned away over his shoulder. He ignores you. The expression is proud and a little weary, not savage.

spots.title: The silk
spots.text: Salmon pink silk, creased and shining, with fine braid along the seams. Each fold has a bright ridge and a soft shadow. This cloth takes up almost half the canvas.

lesson.text: Nothing matches the reputation. A looter on campaign would not ride in a delicate silk tunic, and this one is spotless. The label says “brute”. The picture says elegance, calm, even tenderness. Gérôme seems far more interested in the cloth and the face than in the cliché.
The sitter's name is not recorded. He was most likely a professional model working in Paris, wearing clothes from the painter's own trunks.

Against a plain olive-brown background, with no desert and no story, the work comes close to a portrait. The light falls from the left, slides over the cheekbone and leaves the eye in shade. The canvas is modest, about 81 by 66 centimeters (32 by 26 inches), so the head is close to life-size.
He is armed, though you might not have noticed. A long gun rises behind his back, and a cluster of pale handles pokes up at his waist. Gérôme tucks one more thing into the dark.
Gérôme signed this canvas in a spot where the letters nearly vanish into the background. Can you find his name?

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: “J.L. GEROME” in thin dark capitals, at the left, beside the gun barrel and just above the pink shoulder. It is as discreet as his brushwork.

lesson.text: That quiet signature fits the method. The paint is thin and blended until no stroke remains, so nothing stands between you and the silk. While younger painters in Paris were starting to show off the brush, Gérôme made his hand disappear.

The pale shapes at the right are the handles of weapons carried in his sash. The pair that flare out like ears belong to a type of pistol or blade known for such “eared” grips, often made of ivory or bone.
A title can carry a prejudice that the painting itself quietly contradicts. Here, a man called a brigand is given the stillness and dignity of a prince.

The picture stayed in private hands for well over a century. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York bought it in 2008, and it has since become one of the most admired faces in its nineteenth-century galleries.

quiz.question: What was a bashi-bazouk?
options: An unpaid irregular soldier of the Ottoman Empire
quiz.explanation: They were irregular soldiers who drew no pay and lived on loot.

quiz.question: Where was the painting made?
options: In a camp in the Sinai desert
quiz.explanation: He dressed a model in Paris with clothes brought back from his journey.

quiz.question: What takes up almost half the canvas?
quiz.explanation: The salmon pink silk fills the lower half.

quiz.question: Where is Gérôme's signature?
options: At the left, near the gun barrel
quiz.explanation: It sits in dark capitals at the left, above the shoulder.

quiz.question: Which event was Gérôme invited to in 1869?
options: The opening of the Suez Canal
quiz.explanation: He was among the guests at the canal's opening in Egypt.

facts.text: The soldier looks straight at the viewer with a fierce stare.
facts.explanation: He is in profile, eyes half lowered, looking away.

facts.text: The name bashi-bazouk means roughly “headless” or leaderless.
facts.explanation: The irregulars had no regular command and no pay.

facts.text: Gérôme painted the figure outdoors during his desert journey.
facts.explanation: It was painted in Paris from a model wearing costumes he had brought back.
